name: Tomas Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at Paywell, a company that makes payroll software, the programs that work out people's wages and tax. I mostly maintain old C# code that calculates deductions, and I check that changes don't break anyone's payslip. It's careful, slow work, and I like that. I'm in at half eight, out at five, and I play five-a-side football on Thursdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's predictable. Payroll has rules, and when my code is right, ten thousand people get paid the right amount. What wears me out is how much faster everyone else seems to learn. The others use AI tools; I don't, I've never seen the point, and I'd rather check things myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. Maybe at football I'd say the whole thing calmed down, which is what I expected. I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can carry on. Payroll changes slowly, the tax rules change once a year, and someone has to make sure the numbers are right. A plateau suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep saving. I'd try to get through the internal C# certificate by next autumn so I'm less slow. And I'd probably ask for a pay review, since nothing would have changed to stop one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. I like things to stay the way they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use the AI tools. In this world, does that hold you back at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. If the others are faster with the tools, I'd look slower in reviews. But a payroll bug costs real money, and my manager Helen knows I'm the one who double-checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with your money at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I save most of it. I've got nearly a year of pay put away, and I live alone in a small rented flat. I'd like to buy one in a couple of years, nothing fancy.

say: I'd say at football that the whole thing **calmed down**, as I expected.
I wouldn't post anything **online**; I'd just carry on.
think: Payroll **changes slowly**, so a plateau suits me fine.
Someone still has to make sure the **numbers** are right.
do: Pass the internal **C# certificate** by next autumn.
Ask for a **pay review** once things settle.
feel: **Calm** and relieved that things stay the same.
S0.quote: Payroll changes slowly, the tax rules change once a year, and someone has to make sure the numbers are right.
fieldNote: He values **predictability** above almost everything at work.
He's slower than peers but trusted as the **double-checker**.
Nearly a **year of savings** makes this world easy for him.
His one goal is to **buy a flat**.

steps.text: Pass the internal C# certificate by next autumn
Keep maintaining the payroll deduction code
Save towards a deposit on a small flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to wait and see what actually works. Plenty of companies will rush in and make a mess of their payroll, and I'd say so at work. I'm not against it, I just don't believe the sales talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Checking and coding are both on that list, and that's my whole job. If Paywell needs fewer juniors, I'm the one who doesn't use the tools, so I'd be near the top of the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the flat plan for now and keep the deposit as a cushion instead. I'd cut back on the holiday to Lisbon I've been planning. And I'd wait a few months to see whether the tools actually get payroll right before I touch them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the sort of worry that sits in your stomach on a Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on the tools. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Helen told me directly that I'd be let go without them. Or if I saw them pass the tax-rule tests without mistakes for six months. Then I'd learn them, slowly, the way I learn everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it went badly, what would you do on the first Monday without a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call my older brother Kofi. He runs a small plumbing business and always says there's a van seat for me. I'd probably laugh it off the first week and then actually think about it.

say: I'd say it's **sensible to wait** and see what actually works.
I'd warn that rushed **payroll** systems will make a mess.
think: **Checking and coding** are my whole job, and both are on the list.
Not using the tools puts me **near the top** of any cut.
do: Pause the **flat purchase** and keep the deposit as a cushion.
Wait **a few months** before touching the AI tools.
feel: **Anxious**, a worry that sits in his stomach on **Sunday nights**.
S1.quote: Checking and coding are both on that list, and that's my whole job.
fieldNote: He knows his **refusal** of the tools makes him a target.
His caution shows in **pausing** the flat rather than spending.
His brother's **plumbing business** is a quiet fallback.
He'd only adopt AI after six months of **proof**.

steps.text: Pause the flat purchase and keep the deposit as a cushion
Wait six months before trying the payroll AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready and the government should slow it down. I'm not a political person, but I'd sign something for that. At work I'd say we need to keep humans checking the payroll, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm finished as a developer. A junior who doesn't use AI, when AI can do all the thinking work? There's no argument for keeping me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my brother Kofi for a proper apprenticeship and start within six months, before everyone else thinks of it. I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food. I'd keep every penny of the savings for the two years it takes to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake. I picked software because it seemed safe and steady, and it turned out to be the first thing to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI first, then robots three years after. Does that change where you'd go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. Plumbing is hands-on, under sinks and in cupboards, so I'd have a few more years than the office people. Not forever, but enough to get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your brother offered you a van seat. Would you take it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd swallow my pride. I've always been the one with the clean office job in the family. I'd be the new apprentice at 27 learning from my big brother.

say: I'd say the **government** should slow it down.
I'd argue for **humans checking** payroll for a while yet.
think: I'm **finished** as a developer, and I'd say so to myself plainly.
A junior who never used AI has **no argument** for being kept.
do: Start a **plumbing apprenticeship** with his brother within six months.
Cut spending to **rent and food** only.
Keep all **savings** for the two years of training.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake over a career he chose for **safety**.
S2.quote: I picked software because it seemed safe and steady, and it turned out to be the first thing to go.
fieldNote: The irony of choosing software for **safety** hurts him most.
He'd move fast only because he sees **no alternative**.
Joining his brother costs him some **family pride**.
The **robot gap** makes plumbing a believable bridge.

steps.text: Start a plumbing apprenticeship at his brother's firm within six months
Cut spending to rent and food only
Lean on his brother Kofi for training and work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, slow it down and keep people in the loop. Maybe I'd say it a bit louder, because five years is enough time to actually make rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just later. I'm slow to change, I know that about myself, so five years might just mean five years of telling myself it won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give software two more years and finally finish the C# certificate. Then I'd start the plumbing apprenticeship with my brother Kofi in 2029, so I'm qualified before AGI arrives. Meanwhile I'd keep saving the flat money rather than spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Less sudden, but it's the same wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. Would you still go straight to plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away, no. I'd want to see the first signs at Paywell before I quit, like juniors not being replaced. But I'd set a date in my head and stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'd regret in that five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting too long. I know myself. I'd be the one still at Paywell (his payroll software employer) in 2030, hoping, when I should have been under a sink learning.

say: I'd say again: **slow it down** and keep people in the loop.
Five years is enough time to actually **make rules**.
think: It's the **same ending** as the fast version, just a few years later.
Being **slow to change**, I might waste five years hoping.
do: Finish the **C# certificate** and stay two more years.
Start the **plumbing apprenticeship** with his brother in 2029.
Keep the **flat money** saved rather than spent.
feel: Still **alarmed**: less sudden, but the **same wall**.
S3.quote: I'd be the one still at Paywell (his payroll software employer) in 2030, hoping, when I should have been under a sink learning.
fieldNote: He names his own **slowness** as the biggest danger.
He'd set a private **deadline** to force himself to move.
More time doesn't ease his mood, it adds **temptation to wait**.
He sticks with the **plumbing** route.

steps.text: Stay at Paywell two more years watching for junior cuts
Start the plumbing apprenticeship with Kofi in 2029
Keep the flat deposit saved rather than spent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic. I'd tell people at football to keep calm and plan. That's about as public as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a proper go at software. Ten years is long enough to become a good developer, even a slow one. But I'd keep the plumbing idea in my back pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat in the next two years, because rent is money gone. I'd stay at Paywell and finally learn the AI tools once they've been proven for a few years. And around 2032 I'd decide, software or plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but at a low level. It's a long way off and I like having time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the flat in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. A flat is something solid. Whatever happens to jobs, I'd want my own front door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37 in 2036. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine. 37 is young enough to train. I'd rather change careers at 37 with a flat than at 27 with nothing.

say: I'd tell people at football that **ten years** is plenty, so plan calmly.
Publicly I'd say **don't panic**, and leave it there.
think: Ten years is long enough to become a **good developer**.
I'd keep **plumbing** in my back pocket anyway.
do: Learn the **AI tools** once they've been proven for a few years.
S4.quote: I'd rather change careers at 37 with a flat than at 27 with nothing.
fieldNote: With a decade he finally accepts **learning AI**, once proven.
**Owning a flat** matters to him as something solid.
He keeps a **decision date** rather than a plan.
He stays anxious because his job still ends **eventually**.

steps.text: Buy a small flat within two years
Learn Paywell's AI tools once proven for a few years
Decide between software and plumbing around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no time to do things my way, slowly and carefully. What would help is a proper apprenticeship scheme that pays a real wage, so people like me can move into trades without losing everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are proud of. I'm proud that my code pays people correctly. Nobody's going to thank a machine for that, but I'd miss the feeling.

headlineQuote: Payroll has rules, and when my code is right, ten thousand people get paid the right amount.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old** junior developer maintaining payroll code, careful and slow.
He has never used **AI tools** and won't until they're proven for years.
Nearly a **year of savings** and a flat plan shape his choices.
His fallback is his brother's **plumbing firm**, which costs him some pride.
His biggest danger, he admits, is his own **slowness** to move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to change slowly and carefully.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** scheme with a real wage for moving into trades.
